attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post, written in the first person.

semantics.note: A firm present-tense statement about generative AI adoption. The proposition drops only the word 'really', which does not change the commitment.

contract.note: The plain reading is fair: the context separates use at work from casual use, and the contract tests workplace and recurring practical use. Treating millions of paid workplace seats as significant is the ordinary sense. Q2 2025 is a reasonable window for a claim about the current state.

evidence.note: Dated June 2025, inside the target quarter. CNBC reports OpenAI's own figure of 3M paying business users across Enterprise, Team and Edu. It is a company disclosure relayed by the press, but it directly shows paid workplace deployment in the millions.
Microsoft disclosure of 15M GitHub Copilot users. It does not say whether those users are paid or active, so it is context only.
Representative Pew survey: 28% of employed US adults use ChatGPT for work. Fieldwork ended before Q2 2025, so it is context only, though it is consistent with substantial use at work.

reviews.rationale: The contract's contradiction condition is substantial paid workplace deployment during Q2 2025. e1 reports 3M paying business users in June 2025. Pew (e3) and Copilot (e2) are context, but both point the same way. Under a fair plain reading, adoption at this scale is significant, so the categorical claim of no significant adoption is contradicted.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: 'Once this bubble pops' presupposes, without hedging, that the bubble will pop. Treating that as an unqualified forecast with no deadline is faithful. The promise to ask for an apology is correctly left unscored.

contract.note: Requiring a broad, sustained collapse of the AI trade the post discusses is a fair, ordinary reading of a bubble popping. Ruling out failure for lack of a deadline is correct.

evidence.note: Reuters, Oct 27 2026, before the evaluation date. Reports a crash in China (STAR50 down 40%) but only a 6% Nasdaq drawdown, so it shows a regional collapse, not the broad one the contract requires.
Cornell research summary using prices through April 2026. It covers bubble episodes in individual stocks, not a broad collapse after the post was published.

reviews.rationale: The forecast has no deadline. The early-resolution rule needs a documented, broad and sustained collapse of the AI trade. The evidence shows a regional crash in China and only a modest US drawdown, which the rule says is not enough. The deadline cannot pass, so the claim cannot be contradicted either. It stays unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Firm present-tense statements about GPU economics, LLM returns and product similarity. The paraphrase 'near-identical' slightly overstates 'all kind of work the same way'. The similarity part is vague and largely rhetorical.

contract.note: Reading the claim as losses from operating GPUs and LLMs is fair. The speaker gives no owners, accounting basis or definition of returns, so the result depends on the evaluator's interpretation. The contract correctly refuses to let company-wide totals stand in for returns at the deployment level.

evidence.note: CoreWeave Q1 2025 GAAP net loss of $315M, alongside positive adjusted operating income and EBITDA. These are company-wide figures; they say nothing about returns from GPUs from installation.
Microsoft Q1 2025 consolidated net income covers all its businesses. It cannot isolate returns on AI GPUs or LLMs.

reviews.rationale: Neither item measures returns attributable to installed GPUs or LLM operations. CoreWeave's GAAP loss and positive adjusted margins point in different directions, and Microsoft's profit is consolidated across businesses. No deployment-level or comparable LLM cash-return data is in the packet, and product similarity has no test. The evidence does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words about Cursor in his own post.

semantics.note: The scoreable core is that Cursor/Anysphere is badly unprofitable. The 'sign of things to come' extrapolation has no measurable outcome and is correctly left unscored.

contract.note: Testing substantial company-wide losses relative to revenue in Q2 2025 is a fair reading of 'horribly unprofitable'. The speaker named no period or basis, so the result depends on the evaluator's interpretation.

evidence.note: TechCrunch, Aug 2025. A competitor's founder says margins across code-gen products are neutral or negative. That is an estimate of gross margin across the industry, not Anysphere's net result for Q2 2025.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no financial evidence on Anysphere's company-wide profit or loss for April–June 2025. The only item is a competitor's opinion of gross margins across the industry, which is context. Without matching figures for the period, neither substantial losses nor profitability can be established.
